intent: understand closing line value as a process metric
title: Closing line value measures price quality, not certainty
seoTitle: Closing Line Value: Meaning and Limits
description: Learn how to record and compare closing line value, why the exact market and timestamp matter, and why CLV is useful without proving future profit.
dek: Beating a later market price can be evidence that your process found a better number. It is not proof that the wager should win or that every market improves toward close.
author: chris-habib

hero.alt: Opening and closing price markers aligned on a restrained comparison axis
hero.caption: AI-assisted editorial illustration using generic prices. It does not depict a real wager or outcome.

disclosure: This guide explains a recordkeeping metric. It does not claim that positive closing line value guarantees profit, and it does not present a private WagerProof backtest.
verdict: Track CLV because the price is observable even when a single outcome is noisy. Compare the exact same market, side, and settlement rules at consistent timestamps. Use CLV with calibration, sample size, and complete results, not as a substitute for them.

faqs.question: What is closing line value?
faqs.answer: Closing line value compares the price you recorded with a defined later market price, usually near the event start. It is a price-quality measure, not the result of the wager.

faqs.question: Does positive CLV guarantee profit?
faqs.answer: No. A wager with a better price can still lose, and a strategy can show positive CLV over a small or biased sample without producing durable profit. CLV should be reviewed with complete records, calibration, and sample size.

faqs.question: Which closing price should I use?
faqs.answer: Choose a consistent reference before analysis, such as the same sportsbook's final available price or a documented market consensus at a fixed cutoff. Do not switch references after seeing which one makes the record look better.
